reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / ESE-ENSAT Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Adrenal Incidentalomas
clinicalPearls: The commonest adrenal incidentaloma, discovered on imaging performed for unrelated reasons and, by definition, without clinical or biochemical evidence of hormone excess
Every adrenal incidentaloma requires two parallel assessments: whether it is hormonally active, and whether it looks benign or malignant on imaging
On unenhanced CT a homogeneous lipid-rich lesion with low attenuation is characteristic of a benign adenoma, and contrast washout studies help when attenuation is indeterminate
Hormonal screening includes an overnight dexamethasone suppression test and plasma or urinary metanephrines, with an aldosterone-to-renin ratio added in hypertensive or hypokalaemic patients
A truly non-functioning adenoma with benign imaging features needs no treatment, although interval imaging may be considered for indeterminate lesions
Size and imaging phenotype guide malignant risk, with larger or atypical lesions raising concern for adrenocortical carcinoma
A proportion initially labelled non-functioning are found on testing to have mild autonomous cortisol secretion
reference.pathophysiology: A non-functioning adrenal adenoma is a benign clonal proliferation of adrenocortical cells that does not secrete clinically significant amounts of hormone. Most are lipid-rich, which gives them low attenuation on unenhanced CT. Their clinical importance lies in the need to distinguish them from hormonally active tumours and from malignant lesions such as adrenocortical carcinoma or metastasis, since the great majority of incidentalomas prove to be benign and non-secreting.
additionalDifferentials: Hormonally active cortisol- or aldosterone-secreting adenoma
additionalInvestigations: Unenhanced CT for attenuation and a contrast washout study when attenuation is indeterminate
Chemical-shift MRI to detect intracytoplasmic lipid
Overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test for autonomous cortisol secretion
Plasma free or 24-hour urinary metanephrines to exclude phaeochromocytoma
Aldosterone-to-renin ratio in hypertension or hypokalaemia
Surgical referral if malignancy is suspected
redFlags: Large size, irregular margins, heterogeneity or high unenhanced attenuation suggesting malignancy
Biochemical evidence of hormone excess emerging over time
A history of extra-adrenal malignancy raising concern for metastasis
reference.prognosis: Excellent for a benign, non-functioning, imaging-stable adenoma, which rarely changes; the prognosis worsens only if the lesion later proves to be hormonally active or malignant on further evaluation.
pitfalls: Omitting hormonal screening and missing subclinical cortisol excess or a phaeochromocytoma
Over-investigating clearly benign lipid-rich adenomas with repeated imaging
Biopsying an adrenal mass before biochemically excluding phaeochromocytoma
Ignoring interval growth or new hormone excess during follow-up
references: ESE-ENSAT Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Adrenal Incidentalomas
management: Reassure and avoid intervention for a confirmed non-functioning adenoma with benign imaging features
Exclude autonomous cortisol secretion with an overnight dexamethasone suppression test and exclude phaeochromocytoma with plasma or urinary metanephrines
Add an aldosterone-to-renin ratio in patients with hypertension or hypokalaemia
Characterise the lesion with unenhanced CT attenuation, using contrast washout or chemical-shift MRI when indeterminate
Undertake interval imaging and biochemical review for indeterminate lesions to detect growth or new hormone secretion
Refer for adrenalectomy if the lesion later proves hormonally active or develops features suspicious for malignancy
